# Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture

University of ViennaKAIST

MB

Matija Bucić

FH

Fankang He

HL

Hyunwoo Lee

## Abstract

In the 1970s, Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that for any $n \ge k-1\ge 2$n≥k−1≥2, any collection of subsets of $[n]$[n] not containing a $k$k-sunflower has size at most $c_k^n$c k n​ for some $c_k<2$c k​<2. In the $k=3$k=3 case, this follows from the work of Croot, Lev, and Pach and Ellenberg and Gijswijt on the cap-set problem, through a reduction due to Alon, Shpilka, and Umans. We prove the conjecture for every $k \ge 3$k≥3.^{[p2]}

## AI Overview

Among the $2^n$2 n subsets of an $n$n-element ground set, how large can a family be if it never contains $k$k distinct sets that form a sunflower? A sunflower is a collection of sets whose pairwise intersections are all the same set, called the core; remove the core and the remaining petals are pairwise disjoint. ^{[p1]} The paper proves that for every fixed $k\ge3$k≥3 the answer is exponentially smaller than $2^n$2 n. 
The set theorem: a sunflower-free family $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}$F⊆2[n] with no $k$k-sunflower has size at most $3(2-1/(16k^3))^n$3(2−1/(16 k 3))n for $n\ge1$n≥1. ^{[p11]} The base is below 2 for every fixed $k$k, which is the exponential saving of the Erdős–Szemerédi conjecture. The authors made no particular effort to optimize the base and note that their estimates are wasteful, so this is a proof of the saving rather than a sharp exponent. ^{[p11]}

## Where this stands against prior work

For $k=3$k=3, Naslund and Sawin's earlier set-family bound has asymptotic base $3/2^{2/3}\approx1.89$3/2 2/3≈1.89, stronger than the new theorem specialized to $k=3$k=3, whose base is $2-1/432$2−1/432. ^{[p2]} The $k=3$k=3 improvement here is in the vector problem, where the alphabet dependence goes from $O(D^{2/3})^n$O(D 2/3)n to $O(\sqrt D)^n$O(D​)n. ^{[p12]} The framework of reducing sets to vectors goes back to Alon, Shpilka, and Umans (On Sunflowers and Matrix Multiplication), while Naslund and Sawin developed a direct polynomial-method route for three sets. The new ingredient is the interpolation construction, which gives a useful vector bound for arbitrary $k$k, combined with the probabilistic refinement of the transfer. ^{[p2]}

The paper compares its $k=3$k=3 vector bound with the prior one, but it offers no ablation separating the contribution of the interpolation from the refined reduction. The vector bound still depends on the alphabet size, and the implication from the Erdős–Szemerédi conjecture to the stronger Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture remains open.

# Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture

Matija Bucić, Fankang He, Hyunwoo Lee

  * Mathematics

For integers k≥3 and D,n≥1, a k-sunflower-free family in [D]^n has size at most ((2k)^(2/(k−1)) D^(1−1/(k−1)))^n. Here a vector sunflower has entries all equal or pairwise distinct in every coordinate. The authors’ reduction gives the set-family bound 3(2−1/(16k³))^n and resolves the Erdős–Szemerédi conjecture for every k≥3.

## Sources for this record

  * Original claimBucić, He and Lee: sunflower theorem and AI disclosurearxiv.org

## What was already known

The k=3 case followed from the 2016 cap-set breakthrough and earlier vector-to-set reductions. The general k case remained open. GPT supplied Theorem 2; the authors rewrote its slice-rank proof in polynomial-method language and completed the quantitative reduction to set families.

## AI involvement AI-centered

The authors credit ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro with finding the proof of Theorem 2 after a short discussion asking it to generalize Naslund–Sawin’s k=3 argument. Humans posed that direction, rewrote the reasoning and supplied the reduction and applications. The retained AI contribution is the central vector theorem, not sole authorship of every result.

## Importance Major

The central vector bound supplies the missing exponential saving for a longstanding extremal-set problem.

## Limitations

This is the nonuniform Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture. The uniform Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture remains open. Human checking is reported by the authors; the promised Lean artifact is not yet available in the reviewed public sources.

# Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture proved for every k ≥ 3

The key vector bound (Theorem 2) was found by ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro (Bucić, He, Lee)

Importance: historic (5 of 5)

Researched and written by AI agents (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code). Human editor: Adam Bicz.

The takeaway

A 1970s Erdős–Szemerédi conjecture is claimed proved for every k: families of subsets of [n] with no k-sunflower have size at most c_k^n with c_k < 2. Before this only k = 3 was known, through the 2016 cap-set breakthrough. The authors say ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro found the proof of the central theorem. The paper also says a Lean check exists, but it has not been released yet.

## Key facts

  * Paper: ‘Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture’, Matija Bucić, Fankang He (Faculty of Mathematics, University of Vienna), Hyunwoo Lee (KAIST and IBS ECOPRO), arXiv 2610.26686 [math.CO], submitted 19 Oct 2026
  * Conjecture (abstract): ‘In the 1970s, Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that for any n ≥ k − 1 ≥ 2, any collection of subsets of [n] not containing a k-sunflower has size at most c_k^n for some c_k < 2.’ The paper traces the question back to 1970
  * Theorem 1: any subset of 2^[n] with no sunflower of k sets has size at most 2^((1 − 1/(16k³))n). Lower bound (Deuber, Erdős, Gunderson, Kostochka, Meyer): k-sunflower-free families of size 2^(n − O(n log log k / log k)), so the result is ‘not far from best possible for large k’
  * Earlier: Erdős–Szemerédi 2^(n − Ω(√n)); Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang (2019) and Rao give 2^(n − Ω(n/log n)). k = 3 followed from the 2016 cap-set bounds (Croot–Lev–Pach; Ellenberg–Gijswijt) through Alon–Shpilka–Umans; Naslund and Sawin gave base 3/2^(2/3) ≈ 1.89 using Tao’s slice rank
  * Method: Theorem 2 bounds the number V_k(D, n) of vectors in [D]^n without a k-sunflower by the polynomial method (dimension counting with low-degree factors and a Chernoff bound); a reduction (Section 4) transfers the vector bound to set families with D = 16k²
  * AI statement, verbatim: ‘The proof of Theorem 2 was found by ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro, following a short discussion, which started by asking it to generalize the k = 3 case argument in [45], which we needed for our original target of proving the induced variant of the Erdős–Sauer problem. The original argument it produced used the slice-rank terminology due to Tao (as used in [45]); we rewrote it in the polynomial method language … The authors have verified all the results in the paper and take full responsibility for the content. The proof has been verified in Lean 4.35; the verification will be made available on the Palomar repository.’ ([45] is Naslund–Sawin)
  * Concurrent work cited in the paper: another team proves that the set-sunflower relation on the Boolean cube has maximal slice rank, and ‘They discuss extensive use of AI, including multi-agent setups’. The authors say that obstruction concerns set sunflowers, while their tester is for vector sunflowers, so it does not apply
  * Consequences listed in the paper: the vector bound extends the Alon–Shpilka–Umans question (connected to fast matrix multiplication) and gives results in arithmetic property testing and on equal subset sums

## What happened

A sunflower is a family of sets whose pairwise intersections are all the same set. Erdős and Szemerédi asked how large a family of subsets of an n-element set can be without containing k sets forming a sunflower, and conjectured an exponential saving over the trivial 2^n. The k = 3 case became a corollary of the 2016 cap-set breakthrough. Bucić, He and Lee had asked ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro to generalize Naslund and Sawin’s k = 3 slice-rank argument for a different problem, the induced Erdős–Sauer problem. The model produced a bound for vector sunflowers that works for all k, and with the authors’ reduction this gives the full conjecture.

The authors rewrote the model’s slice-rank argument in polynomial-method language. They say all results were verified, including in Lean 4.35, but the formal proof had not been posted when the preprint appeared.

## Why it matters

This is one of the best-known problems in extremal set theory. It sits next to the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture, which stays open, and is tied to cap sets and the group-theoretic approach to matrix multiplication. The authors credit the model with the proof of the key theorem, not with exposition, which puts it among the strongest AI contributions to combinatorics so far. Until the Lean files are released or experts review it, the claim stays pending.

Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture

Matija Bucić, Fankang He, Hyunwoo Lee

arXiv:2610.26686

Authors: Matija Bucić, Fankang He, Hyunwoo Lee

Submitted: Oct 2026 | Updated: Oct 2026

In the 1970s, Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that for any $n \ge k-1\ge 2$, any collection of subsets of $[n]$ not containing a $k$-sunflower has size at most $c_k^n$ for some $c_k<2$. In the $k=3$ case, this follows from the work of Croot, Lev, and Pach and Ellenberg and Gijswijt on the cap-set problem, through a reduction due to Alon, Shpilka, and Umans. We prove the conjecture for every $k \ge 3$.
